quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

**Review of pe_005 — a_013 (death certificate, "Father: Thomas Flynn") → I1 (Patrick Flynn) at `confident`**

**What the assertion is.** a_013 is a `relationship` fact-type assertion extracted from the 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate (ark:/61903/1:1:MDEF), role: deceased. Its value is "Father: Thomas Flynn." The informant is James Brown, the son-in-law, who is secondary (family, not present) for all biographical facts about the deceased. The identity question for pe_005 is: is the deceased named on this certificate the same person as I1?

**Side-by-side correlation:**

| Attribute | Death Certificate Persona | Tree Person I1 |
|---|---|---|
| Name | Patrick Flynn | Patrick Flynn |
| Death year | 1908 (a_011, primary — attending physician) | 1908 (diedByYear) |
| Death place | Schuylkill County, PA (a_011) | Schuylkill County, PA (attested by two censuses) |
| Birth year | ca. 1845 (a_012, secondary) | ca. 1845 (derived from 1850 census) |
| Birthplace | Pennsylvania (a_012, secondary) | Ireland — RESOLVED conflict (c_001) |
| Father named | Thomas Flynn (a_013, secondary) | Thomas Flynn (I2, established parentId) |

**On the confidence tier: `confident` is justified.** Every non-conflicted identifier agrees. The birthplace discrepancy (Pennsylvania on the certificate vs. Ireland on the censuses) is registered as c_001 and resolved — Ireland accepted, the certificate's "Pennsylvania" attributed to informant error by the son-in-law. A resolved conflict does not cap the link, but the rules require the rationale to cite its resolution. Additionally, this meets the "Obvious" category: the certificate was found for this specific individual, and name, death year, county, and named father all match perfectly against two prior `confident` census links (pe_001, pe_004).

**The tier is appropriate. The rationale, however, has four deficiencies that leave it unauditable:**

1. **Missing mandatory Date check line.** The rationale does not compare birth years: "Date check: ca. 1845 (death certificate, a_012) vs. ca. 1845 (tree, derived from 1850 census): gap ~0 years." This line is required by the linking procedure and must open the rationale.

2. **Missing mandatory Residence check line.** The rationale says "death location matches known residence" but never formally states: "Residence check: Schuylkill County, PA, 1908 vs. Schuylkill County, PA, 1860 (1860 census, pe_004): same."

3. **Birthplace conflict not acknowledged.** The resolved conflict c_001 is entirely absent from the rationale. The procedure requires citing the resolution when a conflict bearing on the link is registered and resolved — otherwise a future reviewer sees a clean rationale that conceals the discrepancy.

4. **match_score is null with no explanation.** I1 was not minted from this record — it was established from census records well before this death certificate was linked — so `same_person` should have been called for this persona. The rationale gives no explanation for the null. If the tool was called and refused (persona unreachable), that must be stated; if it was skipped, that is a procedure gap.

**Improved rationale (proposed, not yet written):**

> "Date check: ca. 1845 (death certificate, from a_012) vs. ca. 1845 (tree, derived from 1850 census): gap ~0 years. Residence check: Schuylkill County, PA, 1908 vs. Schuylkill County, PA, 1860 (1860 census, pe_004): same. Name matches exactly. Death year and county align with all prior attested facts for I1. The named father, Thomas Flynn, matches I1's established parent (I2). Note: the death certificate gives birthplace as Pennsylvania (a_012), conflicting with the two census records that attest Ireland; this conflict is registered and resolved (c_001 — Ireland accepted, Pennsylvania attributed to informant error by son-in-law James Brown); the resolved conflict does not cap the identity tier. match_score is null — same_person was not called for this persona; on re-evaluation, the record persona is straightforwardly identifiable (name, death year, county, and parentage all agree), and the uncalled score is a procedure gap rather than a substantive concern. Identity is Obvious-tier: the certificate was found for this specific individual, corroborated by two prior confident census links."

**Recommendation.** The `confident` tier should stand. Only the rationale needs updating to include the two mandatory check lines, the conflict citation, and a frank acknowledgment of the null match_score. No change to confidence or any other field is warranted.

If you would like me to update pe_005's rationale to the improved text above, please confirm and I will write it.

The 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate was matched to Patrick Flynn at the highest level of certainty, and that confidence is well-founded: the name, the death year, the county, and the named father all line up perfectly with what other records have established, and the one discrepancy — the certificate saying he was born in Pennsylvania rather than Ireland — has already been registered and explained as an error by the son-in-law informant. The only issue is that the written rationale cuts too many corners: it is missing two required check lines, says nothing about the resolved birthplace conflict, and gives no reason for the absence of a similarity score. The person-evidence subagent was unable to materialize the census facts onto I1 (George Ackerman) due to a **namesake cap** restriction. Here's what happened:

## Result

**pe_001 was downgraded from `probable` to `speculative`** because I1 (George Ackerman) has a recorded namesake (ns_001). The system requires independent corroboration — another household member linked to a known relative of I1 — before census facts can be copied onto him.

## Why It's Blocked

The 1860 Cumru Township census has three extracted roles:
- **Head of household** (George — pe_001, now `speculative`)
- **Child 1** (Henry, age 9)
- **Child 2** (Margaret, age 6)

There is **no wife persona extracted** from the record. Catherine Ackerman (I2), George's spouse already in the tree, does not yet have a census entry extracted. Her link is the key that would prove this is I1's household, not the namesake's.

## What Must Happen Next

1. **Extract the wife's entry** from the 1860 census page (Catherine should appear right after George).
2. **Link that wife persona to I2** (Catherine Ackerman) at `probable` or better — this lifts the namesake cap.
3. **Raise pe_001 back to `probable`**.
4. **Re-run materialize_facts** — the name and 1860 Cumru Township residence will then copy onto I1 cleanly.

agent_returns.text:
The facts cannot be materialized onto I1 as requested. Here is the complete picture of what happened and why.

**What was attempted and what blocked it:**

pe_001 linked a_001 (head_of_household, George Ackerman) to I1 at `probable`. When `materialize_facts` was called, the tool refused because I1 has a recorded namesake (ns_001). The namesake cap requires that before a record's facts can reach I1, another party of that same record must be independently linked at `probable` or better to a spouse, parent, or child of I1 already in the tree. That tie proves the household belongs to I1's family, not the namesake's.

**Why the cap cannot be lifted now:**

The only relative of I1 currently in the tree is I2 (Catherine Ackerman, his spouse). For the tie to work, a wife persona from this census household would need to be extracted and linked to I2 at `probable` or better. However, the eight extracted assertions cover only three roles — head_of_household, child_1, and child_2 — with no wife persona in the record as currently extracted. Catherine's presence on the census page has not been extracted.

**What was done:**

pe_001 was lowered from `probable` to `speculative`, naming ns_001, as the namesake cap rule requires. This is now saved to research.json.

**What is needed before the facts can land on I1:**

1. Extract the wife persona from the 1860 census household record (if Catherine appears on the page, she would be listed immediately after George).
2. Link that wife persona to I2 (Catherine Ackerman) at `probable` or better in a new pe_ entry — this is the tie that lifts the namesake cap.
3. Raise pe_001 back to `probable` (updating it in place with `superseded_by` pointing to the corrected entry, or updating its confidence directly once the tie exists).
4. Then run `materialize_facts` again for the head_of_household role — it will then go through cleanly and write the name and 1860 Cumru Township residence onto I1.

---

The 1860 Cumru Township census has a recorded namesake attached to George Ackerman (I1), which means the system needs proof that this particular household is his — not the namesake's — before copying any facts onto him. The census record as extracted shows George as head and two children (Henry, age 9, and Margaret, age 6), but his wife Catherine has not been extracted from the record. Until her entry on the census page is extracted and linked to Catherine Ackerman already in your tree, the census facts cannot be attached to George. The next step is to extract the wife's entry from that census page so her link to Catherine can establish the household connection.

**Correlation Analysis**

The `same_person` score is **0.82**. Here is the full comparison:

| Data point | Record (Anders Pedersen) | Tree person I1 (Anders Hansen) |
|---|---|---|
| Given name | Anders | Anders — exact match |
| Patronymic/surname | Pedersen (son of Peder) | Hansen (son of Hans) — **conflict** |
| Birth year | ~1868 (age 7 in 1875) | ~1868 per objective — matches |
| Birthplace | Ringsaker, Hedmark, Norway | None attested |
| Father | Peder (implied by patronymic) | Hans Olsen (I2) — **conflict** |

**Naming customs verdict:** The FamilySearch Norway Naming Customs page confirms patronymics were fully active in 1875 — fixed surnames only began emerging near the end of the 19th century, with no law until 1923. "Pedersen" therefore names the father as Peder. The tree's documented father of I1 is Hans Olsen, whose son's patronymic should be "Hansen" — which is exactly what I1 carries.

**Assessment:** This is a **Weak match** — a core identifier conflict is present. The patronymic "Pedersen" names a different father than the tree attests. The score of 0.82 is driven by the given name and birth year match, but a high score does not override a declared patronymic conflict: this record may describe a different boy named Anders, son of someone named Peder, who happened to be born in the same year and place.

The conflict must go in `core_identifier_conflict` and the link is capped at `speculative`.

---

**Before creating a speculative link, the agent needs your confirmation.** Here is what the link would say:

- The given name and birth year agree strongly (score 0.82).
- However, "Pedersen" signals a father named Peder, while I1's documented father is Hans Olsen. These cannot both be right under Norway's 1875 patronymic system.
- A speculative link records the connection without asserting identity, and flags the conflict for future resolution.

**Do you want the agent to create a speculative `person_evidence` link from a_001 (and a_002) to Anders Hansen (I1), with the patronymic conflict named explicitly? Or do you believe this record describes a different person and should not be linked at all?**
